children: India’s latest dollar-mobilisation exercise has delivered far more than the RBI may have initially expected. The
special FCNR(B) window, introduced in June 2026
to ease pressure on the rupee and bolster the country’s external account, attracted a staggering $127 billion by the end of August 2026.
Along with another $9 billion mobilised through external commercial borrowings and offshore financial centre routes,
the measures drew in about $136 billion.
The response was so strong that the FCNR(B) scheme was closed a month ahead of its original September 30, 2026, deadline. The latter scheme closes by end of this year.
The second-order consequence

At first glance, this looks like an unambiguous success. Foreign exchange reserves have climbed by around $103 billion since May 3026 to a record $786 billion, while the rupee has broadly stabilised in the ₹94-96 per dollar range.
Yet, there is an important
second-order consequence
: the dollars have created a
very large rupee liquidity surplus in the banking system.
That raises a rather uncomfortable question — should we cheer the spectacular inflows?
The answer is more nuanced than the headline number suggests.
A familiar policy response, but a different root cause
India has historically turned to special dollar-mobilisation measures when external-sector pressures become acute.
The India development bonds of 1991, Resurgent India Bonds in 1998, India Millennium Deposits in 2001 and the FCNR(B) scheme of 2013 were all responses to periods of stress.

The current episode, however, is different. Unlike 2013, when India was grappling with a current account deficit of 4.8% of GDP and the after-effects of the global “taper tantrum”, the present problem is not primarily the current account. The deficit remained relatively benign at 0.4% of GDP in Q1 FY27, even with Brent crude above $100 a barrel.

The pressure instead came from the capital account. Weak capital inflows and elevated outflows had resulted in Balance of Payments deficits for two consecutive years, raising the possibility of a third.
RBI’s scheme to attract inflows is lucrative
The rupee had already depreciated sharply – nearly 15% against the dollar between May 2024 and May 2026 – and had breached ₹96 per dollar in May.
The RBI’s June package therefore sought to address the problem at its source by making it attractive for overseas investors, particularly NRIs, to bring dollars into India.

Under the special FCNR(B) arrangement, banks could offer attractive three-to-five-year dollar deposit rates, with the RBI absorbing the entire hedging cost. Median deposit rates were around 6.5%, compared with prevailing rates of 3-3.5%. With leverage of roughly 9-10 times, estimated investor returns could reach 15-20%.
The market had expected substantial inflows of $75-80 billion, with a tail scenario of more than $100 billion. Actual inflows overshot even that optimistic scenario.
The rupee has stabilised, but not appreciated

The scheme has clearly helped improve dollar availability and stabilise the currency. The rupee has remained largely in the ₹94-96 range, while the RBI’s real effective exchange rate index recovered from 87.1 in May to above 89 during June-July 3026.
This is where the comparison with 2013 becomes revealing.

The 2013 FCNR(B) exercise attracted about $34 billion and was followed by a sharp 9% appreciation in the rupee over the subsequent three to four months. There has been no comparable appreciation this time.

That is not necessarily a failure. It suggests that the measures have primarily provided short-term relief by improving dollar availability rather than fundamentally altering the underlying forces determining the currency.
Beyond the immediate horizon, FII sentiment, crude prices and net FDI flows will continue to matter for the Balance of Payments and the rupee.
Indeed, the RBI appears to have been actively managing the consequences of the inflows. A portion of the increase in reserves may already have been sterilised through foreign exchange operations.
The unintended liquidity problem
The bigger concern lies elsewhere.

When overseas investors bring dollars into Indian banks, the banking system receives rupees in exchange. In a normal environment, this additional liquidity may be welcome. But the scale this time is extraordinary.

Banking-system liquidity has moved from near-neutral levels to around ₹11 trillion. After adjusting for government cash balances, durable liquidity is estimated to have risen from about ₹5 trillion to at least ₹14 trillion — nearly 5% of bank net demand and time liabilities.
Overnight rates have consequently collapsed. The weighted average overnight rate has fallen below 5%, while collateralised market repo rates have traded around 4.5-4.65%.
In effect, India is experiencing a pseudo rate cut - without the Monetary Policy Committee actually cutting the policy rate.
The timing is particularly uncomfortable. Inflation risks are rising, CPI inflation could move towards 6 % in the coming months, and global central banks remain in a tightening environment.
An unintended easing of domestic financial conditions is therefore not necessarily desirable.
Downside risks of the forex flood
Persistently cheap short-term money can also encourage indiscriminate credit expansion, widen the interest-rate differential and potentially weaken foreign portfolio investor sentiment.
The irony is striking:
a programme designed to protect the currency could, if liquidity is allowed to remain excessive, eventually create conditions that put renewed pressure on the currency.
Why 2013 is not the right comparison

The magnitude of the current operation explains why the 2013 experience offers only limited guidance. The $136 billion mobilised in 2026 has generated roughly ₹13 trillion of rupee resources, compared with around ₹2.1 trillion generated by the $34 billion inflow in 2013. The impact on the banking system is therefore about 6.5 times larger.

In 2013, the system was able to absorb much of the liquidity naturally. Currency leakage absorbed a significant portion of the RBI’s foreign-exchange absorption, leaving the system with only a modest narrowing of its liquidity deficit.
The more relevant precedents are therefore demonetisation and the Covid period, when the banking system also experienced exceptionally high liquidity.

But the macro backdrop today is very different. During demonetisation, inflation was below 3%, the rupee was appreciating and the RBI was easing. During Covid, surplus liquidity was an explicit policy objective amid unprecedented global monetary easing. Today, inflation is expected to rise, global rates are moving higher and the rupee remains under depreciation pressure.
The RBI’s difficult sterilisation choice
The RBI consequently faces a difficult balancing act.
It can absorb liquidity through CRR (cash reserve ratio) or incremental CRR increases, but doing so could undermine the very assurances that allowed banks to offer attractive FCNR(B) rates.
OMO (open market operations) sales are more durable but could push government bond yields higher at a time when fiscal borrowing and global rates are already exerting upward pressure.

Forex sell-buy swaps can absorb liquidity temporarily, but they carry a cost in the form of higher forward premia. Long-duration VRRR operations, meanwhile, have attracted limited participation and are better suited to fine-tuning liquidity than dealing with a system-wide surge of this magnitude. Thus, every measure comes with its own cost.

The RBI has now moved towards a more decisive response, announcing OMO sales of ₹1 trillion in three tranches during September. This is an important first step, but the eventual trajectory of liquidity will depend on how aggressively and persistently the central bank sterilises the surplus.
What does it mean for banks and bonds?
For banks, the FCNR(B) inflows are an immediate positive. Deposit growth has surged to 17.8% year-on-year, well above the 11-12% trend prevailing before the scheme.
Between June and August, banks mobilised ₹18.7 trillion of deposits, compared with a historical addition of around ₹4 trillion during the comparable period.

This reduces banks’ immediate dependence on expensive wholesale funding. If credit growth reaches around 16 % by year-end, the additional lending requirement could be around ₹34 trillion, with NRI deposits potentially meeting nearly one-third of that requirement.

For the bond market, however, the picture is less straightforward. Strong liquidity should support lower yields, but heavy government borrowing expected in the second half of FY27, elevated global rates and expensive crude oil exert upward pressure. The 10-year government bond yield is consequently hovering around 7%, while both government and corporate bond curves have steepened at the short end.

Investors should therefore resist the temptation to equate large foreign inflows with an automatic case for buying duration. The more important variable is how many rupees the RBI ultimately allows those dollars to leave behind.

The FCNR(B) exercise has succeeded spectacularly in mobilising foreign currency. The next test is whether the RBI can manage the rupee liquidity created in the process without allowing monetary conditions to ease unintentionally.

The success of the programme, therefore, should not be measured by the $136 billion headline alone. It should also be judged by what happens next to liquidity, inflation, credit growth, the rupee, and the yield curve.
Spectacular inflows are certainly something to celebrate. But in macroeconomics, even a success can carry the seeds of its next challenge.
(Namrata Mittal, CFA, Chief Economist; Varnika Khemani, Economist, SBI Mutual Fund.)
Views are personal and do not represent the stand of this publication.

title: After the Forex Deluge Comes the Challenge: A ‘pseudo rate cut’
